notes.b: Body image is about how you see and feel about your body, not about what your body is actually like. It is shaped by the ideals a society promotes, and those ideals affect who takes part in physical activity.
points: Body image is a person's perceptions, thoughts and feelings about their own body, including how they think others see it. It is a perception, so two people with the same shape can have very different body images.
Body image can be positive or negative, and it is not the same as the body's actual shape or weight. Someone can be healthy and still feel negatively about their body.
Body ideals are the 'perfect' bodies a society promotes. The ideal promoted for women is typically slim and toned; for men, it is lean (low in body fat) and muscular.
Few people naturally match these ideals, so many people compare themselves with a standard they cannot reach, which can leave them with a negative body image.

The ideals draw on dominant notions of masculinity and femininity (the society's accepted ideas of what a man or a woman should be like). There is more on this in Gender socialisation and its impact on participation.
notes.tip: If asked to define body image, give it as a perception, thoughts and feelings about your own body, and not as body shape or weight. Back it with an example to explain it.

notes.h: How body image influences female participation
notes.b: How a girl feels about her body affects whether she joins in physical activity and whether she stays. Two main worries show up: being looked at, and looking 'too muscular'.
points: Self-consciousness about appearance, feeling watched or judged, sweating and revealing kit lead some girls to avoid activity or drop out, especially in adolescence (the teenage years, when body image concerns are strongest).

Fear of becoming 'too muscular' steers girls away from strength training and contact sports (sports with physical contact between players, such as rugby), because muscle does not fit the slim, toned ideal.
notes.tip: When asked how body image may influence participation, use two clear examples, such as feeling watched or judged in revealing kit, and fear of becoming too muscular.

notes.h: How body image influences male participation
notes.b: Boys face pressure from their ideal body too, but it pushes them in a different direction: towards building size, and away from anything that exposes a body that does not fit.
points: Pressure to be muscular pushes boys towards weight training and away from activities seen as unmasculine (not fitting the accepted idea of what boys do).
Boys who feel too small, too heavy or unathletic may avoid team sports and changing rooms, because both put their bodies on show and invite comparison with others.
notes.tip: Exams ask how body image may affect young men's participation as well as young women's, so have a male example ready, not just female ones.

notes.h: Body image as a barrier or a support for both sexes
notes.b: Putting the female and male examples together, the pattern is the same for both sexes: how you feel about your body decides whether activity feels open to you or closed off.
points: Negative body image is a barrier to joining and staying in physical activity for both males and females, because feeling judged or inadequate makes people avoid situations where their body is on show.
Positive body image supports joining and staying in physical activity for both males and females, because people who are comfortable with their body are more willing to take part.

notes.b: The influence runs both ways. Taking part in physical activity can improve how people feel about their body, but some activities can damage it.
points: Positive effect: regular activity improves fitness, competence (feeling able at a skill) and self-esteem (how much you value yourself).
Positive effect: it shifts attention from how the body looks to what it can do, known as body functionality. A body judged by what it can achieve is less likely to be judged on appearance alone.

Negative effect: activities that emphasise weight or appearance, such as gymnastics, dance, distance running, weight-category sports (where athletes must make a set weight) and bodybuilding, can lead to unhealthy dieting, disordered eating (unhealthy eating patterns) or excessive exercise.
Muscle dysmorphia: in males, the belief that one's body is too small despite being muscular, an extreme effect of body image pressure.
notes.tip: If asked how female body image can be influenced by participation, give both sides: the positive effects of fitness, competence, self-esteem and body functionality, and the negative effects in activities that emphasise weight or appearance. Keep the negative effects to a brief statement, with no clinical detail.

notes.h: Media representations of male and female bodies
notes.b: The media (the channels that carry images and stories to the public) are a major source of body ideals. What they show, and who they show, shapes what young people think bodies and sports are for.
points: Media, including TV, magazines, advertising and social media, show narrow, idealised bodies: thin and toned women, and lean muscular men.
Many images are edited or filtered, so the bodies they show are not a realistic picture of typical bodies. A fitness influencer's edited photos are one example.

Female athletes are more often shown for appearance, sexualised poses (poses that present the body as sexually attractive) or personal life, while male athletes are more often shown for power, strength and action.
Social media lets young people compare themselves constantly with idealised images, including those posted by influencers (people with large online followings) and fitness accounts.

Male athletes in aesthetic activities (where appearance or artistic movement is judged) and female athletes in power and contact sports are shown less often, which reinforces ideas about which activities suit each gender.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe two ways media representation of the body may affect young people's participation, and how it may affect young men's participation. Pick two of the points above, such as constant social media comparison or sexualised images of female athletes, and say what each does to participation.

notes.h: Debate: do media representations help or hinder participation?
notes.b: Media images can pull young people towards activity or push them away. A good answer gives both sides and then reaches a reasoned conclusion.
points: Hinder: unattainable ideals lower body satisfaction, and young people who do not match them can feel excluded from activity.
Hinder: when activity is framed as a way to change appearance rather than for enjoyment and health, the motivation is weak and fragile, so people give up when the appearance goal is not met.
Hinder: sexualised images of women can discourage girls from taking part.
Help: images of fit, healthy athletes can inspire young people to start and keep going.
Help: greater coverage of diverse body types and of women's sport shows that bodies of many shapes and sizes perform well.
Help: athletes who speak openly about body confidence challenge narrow ideals.
Verdict: the effect depends on focus. Images that emphasise performance and diversity encourage participation, while images that emphasise appearance and narrow ideals discourage it.
notes.tip: Keep the debate balanced: give both sides, then a conclusion. If asked to discuss whether showcasing lean women and muscular men promotes participation (Higher Level), weigh both sides and finish with the verdict that it depends on whether the focus is performance and diversity or appearance and narrow ideals.

notes.h: Responses to negative body image and media effects
notes.b: Schools and the media can reduce the harm of narrow body ideals. Each response below tackles one cause of negative body image.
points: Media literacy education: teaching young people how images are edited and selected, so they can read them critically and see that they are not realistic.
Representation: media and schools using a wide range of body types in images and teaching materials, so young people see bodies like their own taking part.
Coverage that focuses on skill and achievement rather than appearance, so that athletes are valued for what they do.
Comfortable kit choices that let young people move without feeling exposed, which removes one reason for self-conscious students to avoid activity.
PE that values effort and enjoyment over appearance, so that how the body looks does not decide who feels able to take part.

questions.prompt: 'By showcasing lean women and muscular men, the media helps to promote physical activity among young people.' Discuss the validity of this statement.
questions.model: Case for the statement: lean women and muscular men can inspire. Fit, healthy athletes show young people what training achieves and encourage them to start and keep going. Greater coverage of diverse body types and of women's sport shows that bodies of many shapes and sizes perform well, and athletes who speak openly about body confidence challenge narrow ideals. Case against the statement: the same images set unattainable ideals that lower body satisfaction, and young people who do not match them can feel excluded from activity. Many images are edited or filtered, and social media lets young people compare themselves constantly with influencers and fitness accounts. When activity is framed as a way to change appearance rather than for enjoyment and health, the motivation is weak and fragile. Sexualised images of women can also discourage girls from taking part. Conclusion: the statement is only partly valid. Lean and muscular images can promote participation when they focus on performance, skill and a range of body types, but when they focus on appearance and narrow ideals they are more likely to discourage young people. The media's effect depends on what the images emphasise, not on the bodies alone.

questions.prompt: Discuss how body image influences, and is influenced by, physical activity participation for males and females.
questions.model: Body image influences females: self-consciousness about appearance, feeling watched or judged, sweating and revealing kit lead some girls to avoid activity or drop out, especially in adolescence, and fear of becoming too muscular steers girls away from strength training and contact sports. Body image influences males: pressure to be muscular pushes boys towards weight training and away from activities seen as unmasculine, and boys who feel too small, too heavy or unathletic may avoid team sports and changing rooms. Participation influences body image positively: regular activity improves fitness, competence and self-esteem, and shifts focus from how the body looks to what it can do. Participation influences body image negatively when it emphasises weight or appearance: activities such as gymnastics, dance and bodybuilding can lead to unhealthy dieting, disordered eating or excessive exercise, and in males an extreme effect is muscle dysmorphia. Participation can therefore raise body confidence or, in appearance-focused activities, lower it.
